Advanced Experimental Designs: From Candidate Matrix to Bayesian Analysis

Source: vignettes/v30-advanced-experimental-designs.Rmd
v30-advanced-experimental-designs.Rmd

Purpose

Version 1.1.0 extends the design-first architecture of bayesAgriFlow from randomized agronomic designs to advanced quantitative experimental matrices.

The central idea remains unchanged: design is part of the scientific model, not a formatting detail that is reconstructed after the response has been collected.

This vignette focuses on pre-experimental construction and audit.

The companion vignettes move from the design to posterior response-surface geometry, optimization, pseudoquadratic fertilizer models, design efficiency, and sequential augmentation.

Response-surface methodology was formalized around sequential experimentation and the search for operating conditions by Box and Wilson (Box and Wilson 1951).

The rsm ecosystem provides a mature classical implementation of central-composite and Box-Behnken designs, coded variables, canonical analysis, steepest ascent, and ridge analysis (Lenth 2009).

bayesAgriFlow does not attempt to erase that classical foundation.

Instead, version 1.1.0 adds a Bayesian design and uncertainty layer while retaining explicit geometry and optional interoperability.

Learning objectives

After this vignette, the reader should be able to:

  • distinguish a treatment matrix from a fitted response model;
  • generate circumscribed, face-centered, and inscribed CCDs;
  • generate Box-Behnken designs;
  • construct moderate candidate-set A-, D-, I-, and G-optimal designs;
  • understand coded and natural factor scales;
  • audit rank and estimability before fitting;
  • inspect conditioning, term correlation, and VIF-like inflation;
  • inspect prediction variance, FDS, and VDG summaries;
  • understand why orthogonality, rotatability, and prediction precision are related but not identical properties;
  • import a custom or project-local rsmFlow matrix without creating a hard dependency;
  • preserve the 1.0.0 design -> fit -> inference -> prediction -> decision workflow.

1. Design before response

An advanced quantitative experiment starts with a region of scientific interest.

For nitrogen and phosphorus, for example, the natural-scale region might be:

region <- list(
  N = c(40, 200),
  P = c(20, 100)
)

A response-surface design is usually easier to study in coded coordinates.

The conventional factorial coordinates are -1 and +1, with zero representing the center.

Coding separates geometry from measurement units.

That separation matters because 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen and 20 kg ha-1 of phosphorus should not determine numerical conditioning merely because the units differ.

2. Central composite design

Create a two-factor circumscribed CCD:

library(bayesAgriFlow)
ccd <- bayes_ccd(
  factors = c("N", "P"),
  center_points = 5,
  type = "circumscribed",
  alpha = "rotatable",
  bounds = region
)
ccd
head(ccd$runs)

The object retains both natural and coded coordinates.

The design audit uses the coded geometry by default.

Natural coordinates remain available for field implementation and later response modeling.

For two factors, the rotatable axial distance is based on the factorial portion of the design.

The constructor stores the actual alpha used rather than requiring the analyst to reconstruct it from a table.

3. CCD point classes

A circumscribed CCD contains three conceptual point classes:

  1. factorial points;
  2. axial or star points;
  3. replicated center points.

The coded_point_type column makes these roles explicit.

table(ccd$runs$coded_point_type)

Center replication provides information about pure experimental error and local behavior around the center.

It should be chosen based on scientific and precision goals rather than copied mechanically from an example.

4. Face-centered CCD

A face-centered CCD constrains axial points to the faces of the factorial cube.

fccd <- bayes_ccd(
  factors = c("N", "P", "K"),
  center_points = 6,
  type = "face_centered"
)
fccd

This geometry can be useful when axial settings outside the factorial cube would be agronomically impossible or unsafe.

The trade-off is that face-centered geometry does not reproduce every property of a rotatable circumscribed CCD.

The package therefore reports design properties rather than labeling one geometry universally superior.

5. Inscribed CCD

An inscribed design rescales the factorial portion so that axial points remain inside the specified outer cube.

iccd <- bayes_ccd(
  factors = c("x1", "x2", "x3"),
  type = "inscribed",
  alpha = "rotatable",
  center_points = 5
)
iccd

This is a geometric choice, not a statistical correction after data collection.

6. Randomized run order

Design generation and run-order randomization are deliberately separate concepts.

ccd_random <- bayes_ccd(
  c("N", "P"),
  center_points = 5,
  randomize = TRUE,
  seed = 20260826
)
ccd_random$runs

The seed is stored for reproducibility.

Randomization should still respect practical restrictions that arise from actual field operations.

If a factor cannot be randomized at the plot level, a split-plot or other restricted-randomization structure may be more appropriate than forcing a simple RSM matrix onto the field.

7. Box-Behnken design

For at least three factors, bayes_box_behnken() generates the standard pairwise edge-midpoint construction plus replicated centers.

bbd <- bayes_box_behnken(
  factors = c("N", "P", "K"),
  center_points = 3
)
bbd
head(bbd$runs)

Box-Behnken designs avoid simultaneous extreme settings of all factors.

That property can be attractive when corners of the full cube are costly, unsafe, or biologically implausible.

It is not a substitute for checking whether the resulting quadratic model is estimable and sufficiently precise in the region that matters.

8. Candidate-set optimal designs

Some experiments have constrained candidate treatments rather than a regular CCD or Box-Behnken geometry.

Version 1.1.0 provides a transparent seeded exchange search for moderate candidate sets.

dopt <- bayes_optimal_design(
  factors = c("N", "P"),
  n_runs = 9,
  criterion = "D",
  candidate_levels = c(-1, 0, 1),
  model = "second_order",
  seed = 20260826
)
dopt

The base-R implementation is intended for teaching, reproducible package tests, and moderate design problems.

It is not presented as a replacement for every specialist optimal-design algorithm.

9. A-optimality

A-optimality focuses on average coefficient precision through the trace of the inverse information matrix.

aopt <- bayes_optimal_design(
  c("x1", "x2"),
  n_runs = 9,
  criterion = "A",
  iterations = 10
)

The criterion is model-dependent.

Changing the basis from first order to second order changes the design problem.

10. D-optimality

D-optimality focuses on joint parameter information and the generalized volume associated with coefficient uncertainty.

It is valuable, but it is not identical to average prediction precision.

This distinction becomes important in the design-efficiency vignette.

11. I-optimality

I-optimality focuses directly on average prediction variance over a declared region.

iopt <- bayes_optimal_design(
  c("x1", "x2"),
  n_runs = 10,
  criterion = "I",
  region = list(x1 = c(-1, 1), x2 = c(-1, 1)),
  iterations = 10
)

Changing the region can change the design objective.

That is scientifically appropriate because prediction precision outside the region of use may have little practical value.

12. G-optimality

G-optimality targets the largest prediction variance in the declared region.

gopt <- bayes_optimal_design(
  c("x1", "x2"),
  n_runs = 10,
  criterion = "G",
  iterations = 10
)

I- and G-optimality answer different predictive questions.

13. Audit first

Every generated or imported matrix can be audited.

audit <- bayes_rsm_audit(ccd)
audit

The audit reports rank, number of model terms, conditioning, term correlations, prediction-variance summaries, and information criteria.

14. Rank and estimability

For a second-order model with k quantitative factors, the model basis contains:

  • one intercept;
  • k linear terms;
  • k pure quadratic terms;
  • k(k-1)/2 pairwise interactions.

A matrix that does not have enough independent information to estimate those terms should fail before a posterior model is fitted.

bad <- data.frame(x1 = c(-1, 0, 1), x2 = c(-1, 0, 1))
bayes_rsm_audit(bad)

The package does not repair a rank-deficient matrix silently.

15. Condition number

Full rank does not guarantee comfortable numerical geometry.

The scaled condition number helps identify nearly dependent columns after removing arbitrary measurement-scale effects.

A large value is a warning about precision and numerical stability, not a binary proof that a study is invalid.

16. Term correlation

Non-orthogonal designs can correlate coefficient estimates.

bayes_rsm_audit() reports the maximum absolute term correlation and a correlation matrix when it is defined.

The correct interpretation is not “non-orthogonal equals unusable”.

The relevant questions are how much uncertainty is inflated and whether prediction remains adequate where decisions will be made.

17. VIF-like inflation

The audit also computes VIF-like diagnostics from the standardized term-correlation matrix when invertible.

These values describe the chosen model basis.

They can change if factor coding or model terms change.

18. Prediction variance

For unit residual variance, prediction variance at a design point x is proportional to:

f(x)T(XTX)−1f(x). f(x)^T(X^TX)^{-1}f(x).

The audit evaluates this quantity over a declared region.

Multiply by the appropriate residual variance to move to the response scale under the corresponding classical homoscedastic model.

19. FDS

The fraction-of-design-space summary reports quantiles of scaled prediction variance.

audit$fds

It answers a distributional question about prediction precision across the region rather than reporting only a single maximum.

20. VDG

The variance-dispersion summary groups prediction variance by approximate radius from the coded origin.

audit$vdg

This is especially useful for understanding whether variance is approximately constant on shells.

21. Approximate rotatability

The package reports an approximate rotatability score based on within-radius variability of prediction variance over the numerical region grid.

It is a diagnostic summary, not an exact symbolic proof of rotatability.

The design type and exact theoretical construction remain available in the object metadata.

22. Importing a custom design

A user can provide a treatment matrix directly.

custom <- expand.grid(
  x1 = c(-1, 0, 1),
  x2 = c(-1, 0, 1)
)
custom_design <- bayes_rsm_import(custom, factors = c("x1", "x2"))
bayes_rsm_audit(custom_design)

This is important for historical agricultural matrices and locally constrained designs.

23. Why some historical generators are not invented

The 2002 Agrociencia paper compares Double Square, Double Cube, San Cristóbal, Plan Puebla, several central-composite variants, and optimal designs (Briones-Encinia and Martínez-Garza 2002).

The article reports comparative efficiencies but does not provide every coordinate matrix needed to reconstruct every legacy design unambiguously.

Version 1.1.0 therefore stores the published benchmark and design-status ledger but does not invent coordinates for those legacy families.

A matrix from a verified primary source can be imported immediately with bayes_rsm_import().

This is safer than embedding an undocumented reconstruction.

24. Optional rsmFlow bridge

The project-local rsmFlow package already implements a mature classical design-aware RSM workflow.

Version 1.1.0 keeps interoperability soft:

comparison <- bayes_compare_rsmflow(custom)
comparison$rsmFlow_available
comparison$bayesAgriFlow

If rsmFlow is installed and exports a compatible audit function, bayes_compare_rsmflow() queries it dynamically.

If it is absent, the bayesAgriFlow audit still works.

No dependency is installed automatically.

25. Compare definitions before numbers

Cross-package numerical parity is meaningful only when both analyses use:

  • identical coded coordinates;
  • identical model terms;
  • identical prediction region;
  • identical weighting conventions;
  • identical definitions of A, D, I, or G criteria.

A numerical discrepancy without this definition audit is not evidence that either package is wrong.

26. From matrix to fit-ready design

Once responses have been observed, use the same coded-factor logic to create a Bayesian RSM design.

d <- bayes_teaching_data("ccd")
des <- bayes_rsm(
  data = d,
  response = "yield",
  factors = c("coded_N", "coded_P"),
  order = 2
)
des
bayes_plan(des)

The constructor adds explicit basis columns internally so the native and brms backends share predictable coefficient names.

27. Native versus Stan route

Gaussian fixed-design response surfaces can use the dependency-light native teaching engine.

Student-t response surfaces route to brms/Stan.

The capability registry makes this explicit.

subset(
  bayes_capabilities(c("rsm", "rsm_pseudo")),
  status != "not_supported"
)

28. Design quality is not model truth

A beautifully rotatable CCD does not prove that a quadratic surface describes the biology.

Design quality concerns what can be learned under a declared model basis.

Model adequacy must still be assessed after responses are observed.

29. Practical design checklist

Before field implementation, document:

  1. factors and natural units;
  2. coded transformation;
  3. operational bounds;
  4. design family;
  5. center replication;
  6. randomization restrictions;
  7. assumed model basis;
  8. estimability;
  9. conditioning;
  10. prediction-precision region;
  11. information criterion, if optimization was used;
  12. experimental cost constraints.

30. Reproducibility record

Store the design object before collecting responses.

Save the exact generated run table, seed, factor bounds, and design metadata.

A later analysis should not quietly regenerate a slightly different matrix.

31. What this vignette deliberately does not do

This vignette does not select a single universally best matrix.

It does not fit a response surface and then back-justify the original design.

It does not treat orthogonality as the only quality criterion.

It does not infer legacy design coordinates from incomplete secondary descriptions.

The next vignette starts after responses have been collected and develops the posterior geometry of the surface.

Summary

bayesAgriFlow 1.1.0 adds a reproducible bridge from quantitative experimental design to Bayesian response-surface analysis.

The design layer remains explicit, auditable, and independent of the final response values.

That separation makes later canonical analysis, optimization, and decision analysis scientifically interpretable.

Box, George E. P., and K. B. Wilson. 1951. “On the Experimental Attainment of Optimum Conditions.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological) 13 (1): 1–38. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1951.tb00067.x.
Briones-Encinia, Florencio, and Ángel Martínez-Garza. 2002. “Eficiencia de Algunos Diseños Experimentales En La Estimación de Una Superficie de Respuesta.” Agrociencia 36 (2): 201–10.
Lenth, Russell V. 2009. “Response-Surface Methods in r, Using Rsm.” Journal of Statistical Software 32 (7): 1–17. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v032.i07.
